# Facts_C4_shelf - every shelf-bracket answer number (generated by make_shelf_facts.py; do not edit by hand)

Illustrative values for education. Simplified teaching models: this is NOT a design for real wall shelves.

The same numbers, with units, formulas, spoken forms and the exact printed string, are in facts_c4_shelf.json (keys: shelf_<name> for fixed inputs, V<n>_<name> for variant inputs, V<n>_EpNN_<name> for the episode answers below; the Key column gives <name>). Ep 01, 09-11, 14, 16, 21 and 23 use these numbers but add none of their own.

## Assumptions (every model used below)

1. Shelf load is spread evenly over the shelf; each of the 2 brackets carries half, so the load per bracket acts at the middle of the shelf depth (e = depth / 2), measured from the wall face.
2. Design load F = load per bracket x 1.5 (illustrative design factor for uneven sharing between brackets and for setting items down; course default accepted by the course team).
3. Lever arm measured from the wall face (outside face of the wall flange), not from the bend: slightly conservative and easy to measure.
4. Both flanges carry the same moment M = F x e at the bend (same idea as the course bracket). Stress is checked at the bend: sigma = 6M / (b t^2).
5. Net section (Ep 05, section 2): the section through the upper screw hole, the hole nearest the bend (25 mm below the top outside face; in a redesign, the moved hole). Between the bend and the upper screw no other force acts on the wall flange (worst case: it can lift off the upright there, as in the stiffness model), so this section carries the full moment M = F e (lever arm from the wall face, as above). The clearance hole removes 5.5 mm of the width: b_net = b - 5.5 mm and sigma_net = 6M / (b_net t^2), the nominal net-section bending stress (nominal hole size; the largest hole, 5.6 mm, raises sigma_net by under 0.3%). FOS_net = Sy / sigma_net is checked against the same gate. Section 2 is always the more highly stressed one (sigma_net / sigma = b / b_net), so the strength verdict is set by the lower FOS; the redesign and the thinnest-t rows use both sections. The Ep 07 strength score uses the section-1 FOS (the matrix compares materials, and the ratio between the sections is the same for each).
6. Stress raisers at the bend and holes (including the stress peak at the edge of the screw hole) are NOT in the hand number (pictures only in Ep 06), so the FOS gate of 2.5 must cover them.
7. Stiffness: shelf-flange rotation at the load = M e / (2 E I) (cantilever with an end load: the moment falls from M to 0, so the average is M/2); wall-flange rotation = M Lv / (E I) over the free length Lv from the top outside face to the upper screw (worst case: the flange can lift off between the bend and the screw).
8. Front-edge droop = (sum of rotations) x shelf depth, checked against the illustrative PDS limit of 4.0 mm (course default accepted by the course team). The shelf board is treated as rigid; this slightly overestimates the droop (on the safe side).
9. Screw forces: the wall flange tips about its bottom edge (heel). Screw tension from the moment T_i = M y_i / (y1^2 + y2^2), y from the heel; the heel force C = T1 + T2. The vertical load F is shared as shear by the 2 screws (friction ignored). Shear of the M5 screw is not a concern at these loads and is not checked further. Which way this errs: tipping about the heel is the least conservative pivot (longest lever arms, lowest screw tension); if the flange flexes (prying), the contact moves inward and the screw tension can rise several times. Here T1 stays below a tenth of the preload for every course variant (Ep 08 row T1 / preload; self-checked), so the conclusion "the joint stays closed" holds. The weight of the bracket itself is neglected: slightly non-conservative, and small next to F.
10. Engagement rule (class 8.8 screws, course rule): 1D in steel, 1.5D in 6061-T6, 2D in softer alloys such as 6063-T5. Published guides vary; the screw or insert maker wins. Thread depth must be >= engagement + 1 mm so the screw cannot bottom out.
11. Screw length = grip (t) + washer (1.0 mm) + engagement; pick the shortest preferred length (8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 25 mm, SAMPLE card) that gives enough engagement without bottoming.
12. Stack-up: one direction only (along the line of the 2 holes), worst case. Pitch error of a part = 2 x the position tolerance of one hole. Both screws fit when the total pitch mismatch <= smallest clearance hole - screw diameter. The holes are Ø5.5 ±0.1, so the stack uses the smallest hole, 5.4 mm (the worst case for fit), not the nominal size.
13. Upright holes: CNC-drilled (+/-0.05 mm) at 200 parts or more; drilled by hand from a template (+/-0.25 mm, illustrative) below 200. Bracket holes laser-cut (+/-0.10 mm).
14. Flat pattern: 90 deg bend, inside radius R = t, course K-factor 0.33 (key K_bend in facts_c4.json, the same value as the motor bracket; illustrative, the supplier confirms). Flat length = (A - t - R) + (H - t - R) + pi/2 x (R + K t).
15. Hole-to-bend rule (strict reading, as in Facts_C4): hole edge from the outside face >= (t + R) + 2.5t + R.
16. Bend callout: BEND 90° ±1°, INSIDE R = t (the same pattern as the course bracket drawing, note 2). The angle tolerance is written on purpose: without it the general tolerance (ISO 2768-m) would set a tighter angle on these leg lengths than a press brake holds (typical, confirm with the supplier).
17. Bracket mass (Ep 07) = flat length x b x t x density; the 2 small screw holes are ignored (they change the mass by less than 1%).
18. Material, density, cost and casting prices are typical or illustrative teaching values, not datasheet or quote values.

## Ep 07 - material matrix at the variant thickness (typical values; illustrative costs)

Compared materials (course decision): 5052-H32 aluminium, low-carbon steel (cold-rolled) and 304 stainless steel. No plastic: a plastic bracket needs a ribbed shape, so comparing it at the same flat thickness is not fair.
Weights: strength 0.25, stiffness 0.25, cost 0.20, process fit 0.15, corrosion 0.15. Scores 1-5.
Strength score: 5 if FOS >= 5.0, 4 if >= 2.5, 2 if >= 1.5, else 1. Stiffness score: 5 if droop <= 2.0 mm, 4 if <= 4.0, 2 if <= 6.0, else 1.
Corrosion gate (applied before scoring): a corrosion score of 1 means not acceptable in that environment, so that material is out whatever its total.
Cost score uses relative part cost INCLUDING the finish (5052-H32 bare = 1.0; illustrative): 5 if <= 0.8, 4 if <= 1.2, 2 if <= 2.5, else 1. Process fit: bends easily at R = t: 5 (aluminium, low-carbon steel), 3 (stainless: more springback, harder on tools).
Corrosion score depends on the environment (scored with the finish shown).
Typical densities: aluminium 2.68, low-carbon steel 7.85, 304 stainless 7.90 g/cm^3. Mass is shown for the discussion; it is not one of the 5 weighted criteria.

**Worksheet wording (Ep 07; put this on the worksheet and in the answer key):**

- Why steel can win indoors - stiffness: steel's elastic modulus E (200000 MPa) is about 2.8 times aluminium's (70300 MPa), so at the same thickness a steel bracket droops about 2.8 times less. Droop is usually the first check to fail on this bracket, so steel gets the better stiffness score.
- Why steel can win indoors - cost: cold-rolled steel sheet is cheaper than aluminium sheet (illustrative relative cost 0.7 vs 1.0), and indoors a cheap zinc plating or powder coat is enough, so steel gets the better cost score.
- Why aluminium wins on weight: aluminium's density is about one third of steel's (2.68 vs 7.85 g/cm^3), so the same bracket is about 2.9 times lighter. Weight is not one of the 5 criteria here because a wall bracket does not move; if your PDS makes weight matter (shipping cost, carrying, a weight limit), add it as a criterion and the answer can swing back to aluminium.
- Why aluminium wins on corrosion: aluminium protects itself with a thin oxide skin, so a scratch does not start rust; steel relies on its coating, and a scratch, cut edge or worn spot rusts once it gets wet. In humid rooms steel's corrosion score drops (it can still win there when the aluminium bracket at that thickness fails droop, but then the coating must stay intact: say so in your log), and near the sea it fails the corrosion gate.
- So the matrix answer may differ from the 5052-H32 baseline used in Ep 05-06. That is intended: the matrix can overturn a baseline. Write the reason in your decisions log, and note that the Ep 17 bend radius R = t and K-factor are illustrative course values for both materials, so ask the supplier for the values for your material and thickness.
- Galvanic note: steel or stainless next to an aluminium upright is a galvanic pair; it only matters when wet (humid, outdoor, coastal). Isolate with a nylon washer or sleeve, or keep the same metal family.

- V3: Low-carbon steel, cold-rolled wins (3.35). Steel vs aluminium: steel scores higher on stiffness, cost; aluminium scores higher on corrosion; aluminium is lighter (110 g vs 323 g per bracket).
- V4: 5052-H32 aluminium wins (4.40). Steel vs aluminium: steel scores higher on stiffness; aluminium scores higher on corrosion; aluminium is lighter (90 g vs 264 g per bracket). Close call: Low-carbon steel, cold-rolled (4.35) is within 5%, so treat it as a tie and decide on weight, corrosion margin and supplier.
- V5: Low-carbon steel, cold-rolled wins (4.85). Steel vs aluminium: steel scores higher on stiffness, cost; aluminium scores higher on corrosion; aluminium is lighter (215 g vs 629 g per bracket).
- V6: 5052-H32 aluminium wins (3.60). Steel vs aluminium: steel scores higher on strength, stiffness, cost; aluminium scores higher on corrosion; aluminium is lighter (135 g vs 396 g per bracket). Steel is out on the corrosion gate in this environment. Close call: 304 stainless steel (3.45) is within 5%, so treat it as a tie and decide on weight, corrosion margin and supplier.

## Ep 19 - casting choice for the quantity (illustrative prices)

| Key (V<n>_Ep19_...) | Quantity | Unit | V1 | V2 | V3 | V4 | V5 | V6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qty | Quantity | brackets | 50 | 2000 | 150 | 5000 | 20000 | 500 |
| breakeven | Break-even sand vs die = (die tooling - sand tooling) / (sand piece - die piece) | parts | 2426 | 2426 | 2426 | 2426 | 2426 | 2426 |
| cast_choice | Casting choice | - | sand casting | sand casting | sand casting | die casting | die casting | sand casting |

All variants (typical rules, the foundry guide wins): parting plane through the middle of the width, parallel to the L-shaped side view, so each mould half pulls straight off; the flange faces then run along the pull and need draft (about 1-3 deg sand, 0.5-2 deg die); generous fillet at the inside corner instead of a sharp bend; uniform wall, at least about 3-5 mm for sand and 1.5-2.5 mm for die casting, so a 2 mm sheet thickness does not carry over to a sand casting; machining stock (about 1.5-3 mm) on the wall face (datum A, which also removes the draft) and on the screw-hole spot faces; drill and tap the holes after casting, away from thick, porous zones. Die casting means an aluminium or zinc casting alloy, not your sheet steel: the material changes, so the Ep 06 strength and stiffness checks and the finish are re-run. Sand-cast steel needs much thicker walls than your sheet.

DFA (all variants): kit per bracket = 1 bracket + 2 screws + 2 washers = 5 parts (10 per shelf); a flanged-head screw removes the washers (3 per bracket, 6 per shelf; re-check engagement, because the washer thickness was part of the screw length). The bracket is the same part on the left and the right (symmetric about its mid-width), which is good: one part number. It cannot be fitted upside down without the shelf flange pointing down, so no extra mistake-proofing feature is needed.

Bracket and upright unchanged; kit next revision, same kit number, screw assembly new part number; field: inspect the affected shelves, fit the captive-washer screws where a washer is missing, record the serials | Bend note INSIDE R5 TO R6.5 (the supplier's standard die is inside it) and both holes moved down to 34.0 / 89.0 mm from the top (pitch kept): hole-to-bend 31.25 >= 30.5 at R6.5, also at the drawing tolerances; the shelf rises 3.5 mm, so a new part number SHB-100-8 with the rule 'replace both brackets of a shelf'; first article measures the inside R; the R6.5 samples on the Rev A drawing are rejected (no deviation) | Kit: captive (or bonded) insulating washers under the screw heads, 1 to 4.5 mm thick, so the washer stays in the grip (M5 x 16: engagement 16 - 4 - washer between 7.5 and 11 mm; thinner than 1 mm, or left out, and the screw bottoms), and sealant on the screw threads in the tapped holes of the upright; washer material and thickness from the maker; re-check that the preload holds. One kit change answers both root causes (galvanic corrosion; washer-dependent joint), each stated in the ECO |
